title: Sum of All Subset XOR Totals
directAnswer: Sum the XOR of every one of the 2ⁿ subsets. The O(n) answer: a bit contributes to the total only if at least one element has it set, and when it does, exactly half of all subsets (2ⁿ⁻¹ of them) have that bit set in their XOR. So the answer is `OR(all elements) << (n - 1)` — OR everything together, then multiply by 2ⁿ⁻¹.

remember.pattern: Per-bit contribution counting → OR of all values times 2ⁿ⁻¹
remember.formula:
answer = (a[0] | a[1] | ... | a[n-1]) * 2^(n-1)
# each set bit of the OR appears in exactly half of all subset XORs
rules: A bit can appear in any subset XOR **only if** some element has that bit set — that's exactly the OR.
If a bit is present in the OR, it is set in the XOR of **exactly half** (2ⁿ⁻¹) of all subsets.
So each OR bit contributes `2^bit × 2ⁿ⁻¹`; summed over bits that's `OR << (n - 1)`.
The empty subset contributes 0 (XOR of nothing) — it doesn't change the total.
For n = 1 the formula gives OR × 2⁰ = the single element itself, which matches {} + {a} = a.
whenToUse: Summing or counting a bitwise quantity across all subsets
Any 'over all subsets, total of XOR/AND/OR' aggregation
Problems where per-bit independence collapses an exponential sum to linear
Recognizing 'half the subsets flip a given bit' parity arguments
antiSignals: Need the actual subsets, not an aggregate → enumerate, you can't avoid 2ⁿ
Sum of subset *products* or non-bitwise functions → per-bit trick doesn't apply
Maximum subset XOR → linear-basis / trie, a different technique
n tiny and clarity matters most → brute force is acceptable
remember.takeaway: Subset XOR sum is a per-bit counting problem: every bit present in the OR is set in half the subsets, so the answer is OR × 2ⁿ⁻¹. Decomposing a subset aggregate bit-by-bit is the move that turns 2ⁿ into O(n).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can move past brute-forcing 2ⁿ subsets to a per-bit counting argument, and justify the 'exactly half the subsets' claim.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Brute-forcing all subsets (fine for small n but exponential), or miscounting how many subsets set a given bit and using 2ⁿ instead of 2ⁿ⁻¹.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive that a bit is set in half of all subset XORs, conclude the answer is OR × 2ⁿ⁻¹, and explain why the empty subset is harmless.

problemStatement:
The **XOR total** of an array is the bitwise XOR of all its elements; the XOR total of an empty array is `0`.

Given an array `nums`, return the sum of the XOR totals of **every subset** of `nums`. Subsets with the same elements but different indices are counted separately.
constraints: There are 2ⁿ subsets, including the empty subset
understanding: Consider all 2ⁿ subsets (including the empty one). For each, compute the XOR of its elements; sum those values. The small constraints allow brute force, but the elegant answer comes from analyzing each bit position independently and counting how many subsets set it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the empty subset included?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, but its XOR total is 0, so it adds nothing. Including or excluding it gives the same sum.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are subsets distinguished by index or by value?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: By index — duplicate values at different positions form distinct subsets. The counting argument naturally treats each element independently.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large is n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 12 here, so even 2ⁿ ≈ 4096 brute force is fine. I'll show it, then give the O(n) closed form.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values be 0 or negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Values are positive per constraints. The bit argument would still hold for 0; negatives would need care with the sign bit, but that's out of scope here.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Brute force is fine for tiny n; the per-bit OR trick is the O(n) insight.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Enumerate All Subsets
approaches.whenToMention: State it first to show you understand the definition, then say 'this is exponential; we can collapse it'.
hints: How many subsets are there, and how do you compute the XOR total of one subset?
Use a bitmask from 0 to 2ⁿ - 1; bit j of the mask means 'include nums[j]'. XOR the chosen elements.
Accumulate each subset's XOR into a running sum. The empty mask contributes 0 automatically.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are 2ⁿ masks; building each subset's XOR scans up to n bits, so O(2ⁿ · n). Only a running total is stored, so O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Translate the definition directly into code by walking every subset.

**Encode subsets as bitmasks.** A mask from 0 to 2ⁿ - 1 represents a subset: if bit j is set, include nums[j]. Mask 0 is the empty subset; the all-ones mask is the full array.

**XOR the chosen elements.** For each mask, scan its set bits and XOR the corresponding values into a subset total. Add that total to the grand sum.

**Why this is the honest baseline.** It mirrors the problem statement one-to-one and is correct for any n. With n ≤ 12 it even passes. But it does exponential work, and the interviewer wants you to notice the structure that makes it collapse.

**Where it breaks down.** At larger n, 2ⁿ is hopeless. That pressure is the cue to analyze bits independently instead of enumerating subsets.
approaches.insight: Enumerating subsets re-derives the same bit interactions over and over. The moment you ask 'how often is bit b set across all these XORs?' you stop enumerating and start counting — the path to the linear solution.

pitfalls: Starting the mask loop at 1 and silently dropping the (harmless) empty subset — fine here but a habit worth noting.
Resetting xor outside the mask loop, leaking one subset's value into the next.
Assuming this scales — it's exponential and only acceptable for tiny n.

approaches.name: Per-Bit Counting — OR × 2ⁿ⁻¹ (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'each bit in the OR shows up in exactly half the subset XORs'.
hints: Look at one bit position b in isolation. When is that bit set in a subset's XOR total?
Bit b is 1 in a subset's XOR iff the subset contains an odd number of elements that have bit b set. If no element has bit b, it's never set.
If at least one element has bit b, exactly half of all 2ⁿ subsets have an odd count of those elements. So bit b contributes 2^b × 2ⁿ⁻¹. Sum over bits = OR × 2ⁿ⁻¹.
approaches.complexityReasoning: ORing all n elements is a single O(n) pass; one shift gives ×2ⁿ⁻¹. Constant extra space. This is optimal — you must read every element at least once.
approaches.explanation:
Decompose the sum bit by bit, because XOR acts on each bit independently.

**Fix one bit position b.** A subset's XOR total has bit b set exactly when the subset contains an **odd number** of elements whose bit b is 1. Bits are independent under XOR, so we can total each bit's contribution separately and add them up.

**Case 1: no element has bit b.** Then no subset can ever set bit b in its XOR — bit b contributes 0 to every subset. Notice 'some element has bit b' is precisely 'the OR of all elements has bit b'.

**Case 2: at least one element has bit b.** Say `k ≥ 1` elements have bit b set. A subset sets bit b iff it picks an odd number of those `k` elements. The number of ways to pick an odd-sized subset from `k` items is `2^{k-1}`, and the remaining `n - k` elements are each free (in or out), giving `2^{n-k}` choices. So the count of subsets that set bit b is `2^{k-1} × 2^{n-k} = 2^{n-1}` — exactly half of all 2ⁿ subsets, independent of `k`.

**Combine.** Each bit present in the OR contributes `2^b` to `2^{n-1}` subsets, i.e. `2^b × 2^{n-1}`. Summing over all set bits of the OR factors out the `2^{n-1}`: the answer is `OR(all elements) × 2^{n-1}`, which is just `OR << (n - 1)`. The empty subset contributes 0 and is already accounted for in the half-count.
approaches.insight: The whole exponential sum collapses because 'how many subsets set this bit?' has the same answer — half — for every bit that's achievable at all. Once a single element carries a bit, the parity of all the others splits the subsets evenly, so 2ⁿ⁻¹ is universal and the OR captures exactly which bits are achievable.

dryRun.intro: n = 3, so the multiplier is 2ⁿ⁻¹ = 4. OR the values bit by bit.

java.explanation: OR collects every bit that any element sets — these are exactly the achievable bits.
Each achievable bit appears in 2ⁿ⁻¹ subset XORs, so multiply the OR by 2ⁿ⁻¹ via a left shift.

python.explanation: Accumulate all set bits across the array.
Shift left by n-1 to multiply by 2ⁿ⁻¹, the count of subsets setting each bit.

diagrams.title: OR accumulates achievable bits
diagrams.caption: 5 | 1 | 6 = 7; every bit of 7 is set in half (4) of the 8 subsets.

edgeCases.behavior: OR = a, n - 1 = 0, a << 0 = a; matches {} + {a} = a.
n - 1 up to 11 here; the shift stays within int range given the small values.

pitfalls: Multiplying by 2ⁿ instead of 2ⁿ⁻¹ — double-counts; only half the subsets set each bit.
Shifting by n instead of n - 1 — same off-by-one error.
Trying to sum element values instead of OR-ing them — addition double-counts shared bits.

commonMistakes: Multiplying the OR by 2ⁿ rather than 2ⁿ⁻¹ — each bit is set in half the subsets, not all.
Summing the elements instead of OR-ing them, which mishandles shared bits.
Brute-forcing subsets at scale instead of recognizing the per-bit collapse.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong multiplier (2ⁿ vs 2ⁿ⁻¹)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Only half of the 2ⁿ subsets have an odd count of elements carrying a given bit, so each bit is set in 2ⁿ⁻¹ subsets, not 2ⁿ.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return or_all << len(nums)        # 2^n — doubles the real answer

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Summing instead of OR-ing
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Adding values double-counts bits shared by multiple elements; only the OR captures the set of achievable bits without inflation.
